title: Keynote Address by Professor David B. Wilkins: 'From Law's Empire to Integrated Solutions: How Globalization, Technology, and Organizational Change Are Opening New Frontiers For Lawyers, Clients, and Society'
author: SMU Lexicon

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Wilkins accepts the cluster’s core view that technology should reshape and augment, rather than wholesale replace, legal work. He materially extends the redesign argument by framing lawyers as multidisciplinary problem-solvers who combine legal expertise with technology, strategy, project management and other professional capabilities, while preserving human capital.
qs: Lawyers must thus start to embrace legal work as a collaborative enterprise in which they work alongside other professionals to harness technology, strategy, project management, psychology and other tools to develop integrated solutions to tackle the critical issues of the day, which have become increasingly “legalised”, but yet extend far beyond the law.
For example, the legal business will, at least for the foreseeable future, continue to remain one which depends on human capital, rather than one which is replaced by technology.

kp.k: Global markets reshape domestic legal services without eliminating local differences
kp.d: Ivan Tang Wu Hwan’s report of Wilkins’s 3 August 2023 keynote attributes changes in legal services and clients’ circumstances to global markets and foreign investment, while preserving the importance of local institutions and cultures. This is a qualitative account of structural change, not an empirical finding about AI adoption.
qs: For example, domestic legal markets are increasingly becoming shaped by global markets and foreign investment, though local institutions and cultures remain critical.

kp.k: Three related crises accelerate changes confronting lawyers and clients
kp.d: Wilkins identifies the global health crisis, economic volatility exacerbated by the Russian-Ukraine conflict, and greater emphasis on sustainability, stakeholders and social justice as accelerants of recent change. He argues that these developments increase law’s importance while challenging traditional understandings of legal practice.
qs: These changes have also, in recent years, become “turbocharged” by three related crises: (**1**) the recent global health crisis, (**2**) the volatile global economic system (exacerbated by the recent Russian-Ukraine conflict) and (**3**) the increasing global focus on sustainability, stakeholders and social justice.
Professor Wilkins then observed that these have made the law more important than ever.

kp.k: Lawyers should become multidisciplinary problem solvers
kp.d: Wilkins recommends moving beyond a legal-technician role toward collaborative problem solving with other professionals. His rationale is that complex, increasingly legalised problems require integrated solutions combining law with technology, strategy, project management and psychology. This is a recommendation about professional roles, rather than a measured account of task automation.
qs: Instead of being mere legal technicians, lawyers must now see themselves as problem solvers.

Lawyers must thus start to embrace legal work as a collaborative enterprise in which they work alongside other professionals to harness technology, strategy, project management, psychology and other tools to develop integrated solutions to tackle the critical issues of the day, which have become increasingly “legalised”, but yet extend far beyond the law.

kp.k: Human capital remains central despite technological change
kp.d: Wilkins predicts that legal business will continue to depend on human capital rather than be replaced by technology, expressly limiting this outlook to the foreseeable future. He recommends integrating continuity with change; the report provides no quantified employment forecast or AI-specific evidence for this prediction.
qs: Nonetheless, Professor Wilkins continued, many fundamental aspects pertaining to legal work will not, and should not change.
For example, the legal business will, at least for the foreseeable future, continue to remain one which depends on human capital, rather than one which is replaced by technology.
Lawyers must therefore learn to integrate these competing forces of change and continuity.

kp.k: Harness technology despite its own disruptive effects
kp.d: Wilkins urges lawyers to use technology to address broader disruption, acknowledging that technology itself is increasingly disruptive. He contrasts lawyers’ relative unfamiliarity with technology with clients’ years of digital transformation and reiterates that legal input is only one component of solving clients’ problems. The reported argument concerns technology generally, without specifying generative-AI systems or applications.
qs: To end off, Professor Wilkins stressed that to address the “disruptions” in our world today, we must harness technology (even though technology is itself also becoming increasingly disruptive).
After all, although technology is new for lawyers, our clients have been living with digital transformation for years.
The law is, Professor Wilkins emphasised again, only a part, and often not even the most important part, of what is needed to solve the problems in today’s world.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Wilkins predicts continued dependence on human capital rather than technological replacement, and advocates technology-enabled, multidisciplinary legal problem-solving.
pts.d: Ivan Tang Wu Hwan's report attributes these positions to Professor David B. Wilkins. The report discusses technology generally; despite the conference's reference to GPT, it contains no specific claim about an AI system or its capabilities. Wilkins's continuity prediction is that the legal business will remain human-capital-dependent for the foreseeable future. His accompanying prescription is that lawyers move beyond being legal technicians and collaborate with other professionals, using technology alongside other tools to deliver integrated solutions. These are a prediction and a professional prescription, not reported measurements of AI's effects.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The basis offered is Wilkins's expert argument and contextual observations, not empirical evidence about AI performance or displacement.
pts.d: The report identifies Wilkins's Harvard Law School and Center on the Legal Profession roles. It presents his reasoning that complex client problems require more than legal expertise and that clients already operate amid digital transformation. It supplies no data, benchmarks, named deployment cases, or quantitative employment evidence supporting the human-capital prediction or the benefits of integrated solutions. The supporting quotations are the reporter's account of Wilkins's remarks, not an independently supplied speech transcript.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The human-capital prediction is limited to the foreseeable future; the call for collaborative, technology-enabled practice is immediate.
pts.d: The remarks were delivered on 3 August 2023. No quantified forecast horizon or adoption schedule is given. Continued human dependence is expressly qualified by 'at least for the foreseeable future.' The need to harness technology and work across disciplines is framed as a response to present disruptions and complex problems extending beyond law, not as a forecast of complete automation.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Lawyers must adapt their working role, other professionals become collaborators, and clients' complex problems become the focus of integrated services.
pts.d: The claims concern lawyers and the legal business broadly, without distinguishing firm size, seniority, practice area, or provider model. Lawyers remain central as human contributors but are asked to combine legal expertise with technology and other disciplines. Clients are described as already experiencing digital transformation and needing solutions that extend beyond law. Although the panel reportedly discussed smaller firms and legal education, the article does not state substantive predictions about those groups.
